method: The anchored claim register distinguishes primary biblical statements, individual museum objects and scholarly edited cuneiform records. Individual Middle Assyrian texts are linked by collection, edition, CDLI identifier and specified lines; broad institutional sources serve as context, not substitute proof of damaged signs, personal identities or completed specialist translation. All claims remain awaiting documented independent specialist review.

claims.anchor: Isaiah 20:1 refers to the year in which the Tartan came to Ashdod
claims.claim: Isaiah 20:1 names Sargon as king of Assyria and describes his official's action at Ashdod.
claims.limitation: Sargon's identity is named in the biblical account; the Assyrian history source supplies context, not automatic proof of every detail in Isaiah.

claims.anchor: The text calls the commander Tartan
claims.claim: The commander is called Tartan in the retained translation of Isaiah 20:1.
claims.limitation: Tartan can denote an office title. The specialist notes address terminology, not a unique personal identification.

claims.anchor: Isaiah 20:2-4 describes
claims.claim: Isaiah 20:2-4 presents an enacted prophetic sign concerning Egypt and Cush.
claims.limitation: A prophetic text reporting a sign is not independently verified evidence that all predicted events occurred as described.

claims.anchor: 2 Kings 18:13 records
claims.claim: 2 Kings 18:13 reports Sennacherib's attack on fortified cities of Judah.
claims.limitation: The RINAP corpus is a comparison route; individual inscription passages and campaign chronology still need direct alignment.

claims.anchor: Verses 14-16 describe
claims.claim: 2 Kings 18:14-16 reports tribute involving silver and gold from Hezekiah.
claims.limitation: Do not silently harmonise the biblical amounts or circumstances with Assyrian royal accounts.

claims.anchor: In 2 Kings 18:26 and Isaiah 36:11
claims.claim: The Judean officials request that the Assyrian representative speak Aramaic rather than the language of Judah.
claims.limitation: The stated language choice does not identify modern spoken varieties or establish how every Assyrian spoke.

claims.anchor: Verses 35-37 record the angel
claims.claim: 2 Kings 19:35-37 reports the destruction of 185,000 in the Assyrian camp and Sennacherib's return to Nineveh.
claims.limitation: This is a claim about what the biblical text records. The number and divine agency are not independently archaeologically verified by this entry.

claims.anchor: 2 Kings 19:36-37 says that Sennacherib returned
claims.claim: 2 Kings 19:36-37 and Isaiah 37:37-38 describe Sennacherib's death and Esar Haddon's succession.
claims.limitation: Names and succession are reported in the cited passages. Independent succession records still require claim-specific inspection.

claims.anchor: 2 Kings 17:3 names Shalmaneser
claims.claim: 2 Kings 17:3 names Shalmaneser in Hoshea's tribute relationship with Assyria.
claims.limitation: The verse naming a king must be distinguished from assigning the final capture of Samaria to that ruler.

claims.anchor: 2 Kings 18:9-12 recounts the same siege
claims.claim: 2 Kings 18:9-12 reports the siege and fall of Samaria with regnal-year coordinates.
claims.limitation: An absolute BCE date and attribution between Shalmaneser V and Sargon II require extra-biblical evidence.

claims.section: The subject named at the start
claims.anchor: Nahum 1:1 identifies the work
claims.claim: Nahum 1:1 identifies the prophecy as an oracle concerning Nineveh.
claims.limitation: This identifies the literary subject. It does not itself establish the calendar year in which Nineveh fell.

claims.anchor: Isaiah 19:25 names Egypt
claims.claim: Isaiah 19:23-25 presents Egypt, Assyria and Israel together in a vision of blessing.
claims.limitation: Theological interpretations of fulfilment must be labelled as interpretations, rather than presented as dated geopolitical outcomes.

claims.anchor: Dur-Sharrukin, at modern Khorsabad, was built as a capital by Sargon II
claims.claim: Dur-Sharrukin at Khorsabad was founded as a royal capital under Sargon II.
claims.limitation: The public archaeological overview supports the introductory association; individual construction dates and phases remain to be checked against excavations and inscriptions.

claims.anchor: UNESCO records a revival under the Parthians
claims.claim: UNESCO records a later Parthian revival at Ashur.
claims.limitation: A later occupation phase is not evidence of uninterrupted institutions or unchanged identity across all intervening periods.

claims.anchor: object 66.245.10
claims.claim: The Met catalogues a caravan-account tablet under object number 66.245.10.
claims.limitation: The museum object record establishes the attributed object and catalogue context, not a comprehensive reconstruction of Old Assyrian commerce.

claims.section: A monument with a precise identity
claims.anchor: The British Museum identifies it with inventory number 1848,1104.1
claims.claim: The Black Obelisk is a Shalmaneser III royal monument catalogued as 1848,1104.1.
claims.limitation: The museum's catalogue context establishes the object identification, not all the military events claimed in the royal inscriptions.

claims.section: The name Jehu and the House of Omri
claims.anchor: The second register names Jehu in connection with tribute from Israel
claims.claim: The monument associates Jehu of Israel with tribute and the Assyrian designation House of Omri.
claims.limitation: Assyrian dynastic geography is not evidence of Jehu's biological parentage or a complete chronology of his accession.

claims.anchor: 2 Kings 9:1-13 recounts the anointing of Jehu
claims.claim: 2 Kings 9:1-13 reports the anointing and proclamation of Jehu.
claims.limitation: The Obelisk supplies independent testimony about tribute, not the prophetic commission of 2 Kings.

claims.anchor: The British Museum catalogues the Taylor Prism as object 91032
claims.claim: The British Museum catalogues the Taylor Prism under object number 91032.
claims.limitation: The accession identifies an object, not the entire chronology of the narrated Judah campaign.

claims.anchor: the inscription does not explicitly describe a siege of Jerusalem
claims.claim: The Israel Museum notes that the Assyrian prism does not explicitly describe a siege of Jerusalem.
claims.limitation: An omission is not positive proof that Jerusalem experienced no threat; the biblical account uses a different genre and perspective.

claims.section: An archaeological sequence, not a photograph
claims.anchor: Panel 124904 represents the beginning of the assault on Lachish
claims.claim: British Museum panel 124904 depicts the beginning of the Assyrian assault on Lachish.
claims.limitation: The panel is palace propaganda and not a neutral photograph or exact operational reconstruction.

claims.section: Prisoners and the city after assault
claims.anchor: British Museum panel 124908 depicts prisoners, carried goods
claims.claim: British Museum panel 124908 depicts Lachish prisoners and transported goods.
claims.limitation: Royal reliefs do not record every captive's identity or experience.

claims.anchor: Isaiah 20:1 names Sargon king of Assyria
claims.claim: Isaiah 20:1 explicitly names Sargon as king of Assyria in the account of Ashdod.
claims.limitation: Royal Annals form a separate witness; specialist alignment of individual inscription lines remains pending.

claims.anchor: 2 Kings 17:3-6 names Shalmaneser king of Assyria
claims.claim: 2 Kings 17:3-6 reports Shalmaneser and the events leading to Samaria's fall and deportation.
claims.limitation: This does not by itself settle the disputed relationship between Shalmaneser V and Sargon II's reign.

claims.section: Israel and the east of the Jordan
claims.anchor: 2 Kings 15:29 reports Tiglath-pileser taking northern places
claims.claim: 2 Kings 15:29 reports an Assyrian campaign and removal of northern populations.
claims.limitation: One verse is not a complete list of deportees or their later settlement experience.

claims.section: Identify the tablet, not just the date
claims.anchor: The British Museum catalogues tablet 21901, accession 1896,0409.6
claims.claim: British Museum 21901 (1896,0409.6) is a Babylonian Chronicle whose surviving copy postdates 612 BCE.
claims.limitation: Object dating and date of the narrated fall of Nineveh differ; no inscription-line comparison has been independently reviewed.

claims.anchor: Nahum 1:1 introduces an oracle concerning Nineveh
claims.claim: Nahum 1:1 names an oracle concerning Nineveh.
claims.limitation: The prophetic oracle and Babylonian chronicle are different genres, and corroborating the date is not proof of every poetic image.

claims.section: An archive in thousands of pieces
claims.anchor: more than 3,000 cuneiform pieces
claims.claim: The ATMAP/TCMA source catalogue describes a Middle Assyrian corpus of over 3,000 cuneiform pieces.
claims.limitation: The aggregate catalogue describes surviving textual records, not all original records or a population census.

claims.anchor: Genesis 10:8-12 and 10:22 provide biblical accounts of Asshur and named cities
claims.claim: Genesis 10:8-12 and 10:22 provide biblical references to Asshur and early Assyrian geography.
claims.limitation: The passages are not dated Middle Assyrian administrative tablets and cannot identify an excavated thirteenth-century archive.

claims.anchor: Dūr-Katlimmu, identified with Tell Sheikh Hamad on the lower Habur
claims.claim: Tell Sheikh Hamad is identified with the ancient city Dūr-Katlimmu on the lower Habur.
claims.limitation: The site also includes later occupation; this identification does not make every tablet Middle Assyrian.

claims.anchor: 666 registered fragmentary cuneiform tablets in a sealed deposit
claims.claim: The Harvard-supported excavation study describes 666 registered tablet fragments in a specific Dūr-Katlimmu archival deposit.
claims.limitation: Fragments are an excavation inventory, not an estimate of individuals, deliveries or a complete ancient archive.

claims.anchor: The Middle Assyrian Laws survive in a set of cuneiform tablets
claims.claim: The Middle Assyrian Laws survive as a corpus of cuneiform tablets rather than a complete modern legal code.
claims.limitation: Prescriptive texts cannot establish actual enforcement frequency without practice records.

claims.section: Veiling as a marker of status
claims.anchor: Frederick Mario Fales's study examines Middle Assyrian requirements and prohibitions associated with the veil
claims.claim: Fales distinguishes Middle Assyrian veil/status prescriptions from a more varied documentary practice.
claims.limitation: The modern argument concerns available texts, not an exhaustive census of women's experience or direct evidence for later communities.

claims.anchor: Deuteronomy 24:1-4 and other biblical legal texts belong to their own textual tradition
claims.claim: Deuteronomy 24:1-4 belongs to the Bible's legal tradition and is not an Assyrian legal statute.
claims.limitation: Different textual traditions and contexts may share subject matter without borrowing or uniform interpretation.

claims.anchor: ATMAP's catalogues distinguish types such as receipts, allocations, lists and sale transactions
claims.claim: ATMAP distinguishes different ancient document types at separately identified findspots.
claims.limitation: Catalogue descriptors are entry points to specific tablets, not proof of the terms of every transaction.

claims.anchor: Specialists such as Hervé Reculeau have compared ancient administrative correspondence with royal representations of water projects
claims.claim: Scholarship on Middle Assyrian water management compares administrative texts with royal irrigation claims.
claims.limitation: A regional study does not give verified yields or canal measurements for every Middle Assyrian settlement.

claims.anchor: The Middle Assyrian corpus provides a route to such documents
claims.claim: The Middle Assyrian editorial corpus and its bibliography document the study of personnel and ration allocations.
claims.limitation: An allocated ration is not proof of delivery, adequate food, a worker's status or a representative working day.

claims.section: The meaning of a seal impression
claims.anchor: The Harvard-supported Dūr-Katlimmu research identifies numerous seal images and thousands of clay safety devices
claims.claim: Archaeological study identifies seal images and clay sealings in the Dūr-Katlimmu archival complex.
claims.limitation: An image or sealing does not independently identify every human transaction or certify that goods arrived.

claims.anchor: ATMAP's Laws and Scholarly Tablets catalogue includes rituals, incantations, learned works and other texts
claims.claim: The specialist Middle Assyrian corpus includes texts classified as rituals, incantations and scholarly writing.
claims.limitation: Text classification does not establish how frequently a rite occurred in the population.

claims.section: Scripture on Assyrian worship in its own setting
claims.anchor: 2 Kings 19:37 mentions a temple in connection with the death of Sennacherib
claims.claim: 2 Kings 19:37 reports a temple in connection with Sennacherib's death.
claims.limitation: The passage concerns a Neo-Assyrian king and is not direct evidence for Middle Assyrian ritual practices.

claims.anchor: ATMAP's Tell Taban catalogue presents examples of these distinct document genres
claims.claim: The Tell Taban editorial catalogue includes separately classified letters, receipts and allocations.
claims.limitation: A catalogue genre does not by itself establish whether a particular shipment arrived.

claims.anchor: The ATMAP/TCMA edition identifies KAJ 247 as CDLI P282259, collection VAT 08971, with excavation label Ass 144
claims.claim: KAJ 247 is CDLI P282259, VAT 08971, from Aššur's M 09 archive.
claims.limitation: The receipt designation and worker vocabulary remain qualified in the consulted edition.

claims.anchor: The source edition describes one pair of palace-associated shoes under the charge of a named great steward, an
claims.claim: A Middle Assyrian palace footwear record names a recipient described as a hostage.
claims.limitation: The edition marks the campaign context as uncertain; it does not establish the person's later fate.

claims.section: Barley, a horse and a named recipient
claims.anchor: The edited obverse describes a barley quantity in traditional measures as a ration for a horse attached to a s
claims.claim: A single barley receipt connects a service horse and a named recipient.
claims.limitation: Ancient units and the recorded receipt do not establish the amount actually consumed or all horse provisioning.

claims.anchor: The edited text gives a barley distribution described for ten days and enumerates several separate sets of peo
claims.claim: The ration edition lists distinct sets of personnel guarding the inner city.
claims.limitation: The account's ten-day duration is not a modern annual nutritional survey.

claims.anchor: The edited beginning reports a substantial lead quantity, names parties associated with it and connects the ob
claims.claim: KAJ 144 links a quantity of lead with a house-related sale or obligation.
claims.limitation: The receipt genre and damaged phrases remain uncertain and the legal result is not known.

claims.anchor: The ATMAP/TCMA edition of Billa 30 identifies CDLI P282711 and collection UM 33-58-133, from the Aššur-kašid a
claims.claim: The receipt Billa 30 comes from the Ashur-kashid archive at Tell Billa.
claims.limitation: Some names and the obligation wording are broken or editorially uncertain.

claims.anchor: The edition's opening passage records forty sacks of straw associated with the palace and an institutional cha
claims.claim: The edited obverse records forty sacks of straw in palace custody.
claims.limitation: A recorded quantity does not prove actual delivery or a regional agricultural yield.

claims.anchor: The Metropolitan Museum identifies object 62.85.3 as a Middle Assyrian clay cuneiform administrative tablet im
claims.claim: The Met catalogues 62.85.3 as a Middle Assyrian tablet with two cylinder-seal impressions.
claims.limitation: The catalogue does not provide a verified tablet transcription or exact findspot.

claims.section: A tablet with two historical dates
claims.anchor: The British Museum identifies this as tablet 21901, registration 1896,0409.6, a Babylonian Chronicle that narr
claims.claim: British Museum 21901 is a late copy of a chronicle narrating Nineveh's fall.
claims.limitation: The surviving tablet dates later than the historical events it describes.

claims.anchor: The English edition associates the opening obverse with a group of twenty-two workers and an event interpreted
claims.claim: The published text refers to a group of workers in a temple-related account.
claims.limitation: The precise worker term and event are uncertain; cannot infer voluntary participation.

claims.anchor: The Met labels the object's digital image Public Domain under its Open Access framework.
claims.claim: The Met states that the object image is Public Domain.
claims.limitation: Public-domain image status does not establish a scholarly Akkadian transcription.

claims.section: Read the Bible as a distinct witness
claims.anchor: Nahum 1:1 names Nineveh in a prophetic oracle, and Zephaniah 2:13-15 speaks of the destruction of the Assyrian
claims.claim: Nahum 1:1 introduces a prophetic account concerning Nineveh.
claims.limitation: A Babylonian military chronicle does not prove every prophetic image or theological claim.
